Rifa Ferzana 
Abstract 
Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly achieve expert -level predictive accuracy 
across healthcare tasks, yet their real -world clinical impact remains inconsistent. Prior 
studies demonstrate that improvements in model performance often fail to tr anslate into 
improved patient outcomes—a disconnect this paper terms the allocation gap. We provide a 
decision-theoretic explanation for this phenomenon by formali sing healthcare delivery as a 
scarcity-constrained stochastic allocation problem. Within this framework, AI functions not 
as an autonomous decision -maker but as  decision infrastructure  that improves outcomes 
through utility estimation, variance reduction  and information prioriti sation. We employ 
formal tools from constrained optimi sation and Markov decision processes (MDPs) to 
analyse how improved estimation alters optimal resource allocation under binding capacity 
constraints. A controlled synthetic triage simulation demonstrates that  allocation-aware 
policies—which explicitly optimi se for constrained utility —outperform conventional risk -
threshold policies by 18–25% in realised utility, even when predictive accuracy is identical. 
The framework provides a principled basis for evaluating, deploying  and governing 
healthcare AI beyond task -level metrics, with direct implications for resource -constrained 
clinical environments. 
Keywords: Healthcare AI, Resource Allocation, Decision Theory, Constrained Optimi sation, 
Value of Information, MDPs, Clinical Deployment

inconsistent improvements in patient outcomes (Kelly et al. 2019; Nagendran et al. 2020). 
This persistent discr epancy suggests that predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for real -
world impact. 
Healthcare systems operate under persistent scarcity: finite clinician time, limited diagnostic 
and therapeutic capacity  and irreversible decision windows. Under such conditions, the 
central challenge is not prediction per se but allocation—determining which patients receive 
which limited resources, when and in what sequence. This paper reframes healthcare

7. Conclusion and Future Directions 
Healthcare systems fail not due to lack of intelligence but because scarcity forces difficult

A. The SMARt Autonomy Model: Formalizing State-Based 
Regulation 
Building upon the structural limitations identified in Sections I and II, in this section, the SMARt Autonomy Model is introduced 
as a formal regulatory layer for agentic systems. Modern AI increasingly operates in domains where expert human judgment, tac it 
knowledge, and contextual evaluation remain irreplaceable. Effective intelligent systems must therefore be designed for augmentation 
- amplifying human evaluative strengths while utilizing machine computation - rather than aiming for total operational replacement 
(as illustrated in Figure 1). However, without formalized autonomy regulation, agents tend toward ungrounded continuity when 
internal epistemic confidence degrades.  To mitigate this, SMARt operationalizes observable model behaviors as explicit state -
transition triggers. For instance, internal heuristic actions such as query expansion, prompt rewriting, or recursive task decomposition 
are treated not merely as reasoning tactics, but as probes - measurable indicators of rising internal uncertainty. Rather than permitting 
continuous generation under these conditions, SMARt utilizes these probes as hard constraints to force a transition into a suspended, 
reflective mode until grounding is reestablished. Similarly, behaviors requiring external verification, query routing, or hybrid search 
function as assisted indicators. These signal a knowledge gap that exceeds internal recovery capabilities, mandating a transition into 
an Assisted state where the agent integrates external grounding before proceeding. By converting heuristic reasoning behaviors into 
structural transition triggers, SMARt formalizes the precise lifecycle of when autonomous action is authorized, suspended, escalated, 
or revoked.

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Decision-Theoretic Framework for Allocation-Aware Healthcare AI
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06161v1
published: 2026-01-06T20:42:10Z
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly achieve expert-level predictive accuracy in healthcare, yet improvements in model performance often fail to produce corresponding gains in patient outcomes. We term this disconnect the allocation gap and provide a decision-theoretic explanation by modelling healthcare delivery as a stochastic allocation problem under binding resource constraints. In this framework, AI acts as decision infrastructure that estimates utility rather than making autonomous decisions. Using constrained optimisation and Markov decision processes, we show how improved estimation affects optimal allocation under scarcity. A synthetic triage simulation demonstrates that allocation-aware policies substantially outperform risk-threshold approaches in realised utility, even with identical predictive accuracy. The framework provides a principled basis for evaluating and deploying healthcare AI in resource-constrained settings.

title: An agent-based intelligent environmental monitoring system
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0407024v1
published: 2004-07-10T11:06:57Z
summary: Fairly rapid environmental changes call for continuous surveillance and on-line decision making. There are two main areas where IT technologies can be valuable. In this paper we present a multi-agent system for monitoring and assessing air-quality attributes, which uses data coming from a meteorological station. A community of software agents is assigned to monitor and validate measurements coming from several sensors, to assess air-quality, and, finally, to fire alarms to appropriate recipients, when needed. Data mining techniques have been used for adding data-driven, customized intelligence into agents. The architecture of the developed system, its domain ontology, and typical agent interactions are presented. Finally, the deployment of a real-world test case is demonstrated.

title: SWEnergy: An Empirical Study on Energy Efficiency in Agentic Issue Resolution Frameworks with SLMs
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09543v2
published: 2025-12-10T11:28:48Z
summary: Context. LLM-based autonomous agents in software engineering rely on large, proprietary models, limiting local deployment. This has spurred interest in Small Language Models (SLMs), but their practical effectiveness and efficiency within complex agentic frameworks for automated issue resolution remain poorly understood.
  Goal. We investigate the performance, energy efficiency, and resource consumption of four leading agentic issue resolution frameworks when deliberately constrained to using SLMs. We aim to assess the viability of these systems for this task in resource-limited settings and characterize the resulting trade-offs.

The SLM's limited reasoning was the bottleneck for success, but the framework's design was the bottleneck for efficiency.

Current agentic frameworks, designed for powerful LLMs, fail to operate efficiently with SLMs. We find that framework architecture is the primary driver of energy consumption, but this energy is largely wasted due to the SLMs' limited reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) and agent systems increasingly support scientific discovery across domains. Yet the literature remains fragmented around isolated tasks, with limited attention to how components form integrated workflows. Here, we introduce exploration, hypothesis generation, and testing (EXHYTE) as an empirical workflow abstraction for reviewing AI-assisted scientific discovery. We mapped a corpus of recent studies to EXHYTE stages and substages to identify recurring strategies, workflow connections, and capability gaps. The analysis shows strong progress in exploration, especially retrieval, knowledge assembly, and representation learning as well as growing capacity for hypothesis and idea generation. The central bottleneck remains the transition from hypothesis or idea generation to executable experimental or comp

led prioritization, testing, and refinement across chemistry, materials, biomedicine, and general scientific reasoning.
Discussion and future outlook
This survey synthesizes recent work on AI for scientific discovery through the EXHYTE framework, an operational workflow lens for organizing how LLMs and agentic systems support (or approximate)
Explore
,
Hypothesize
, and
Test
functions. Using this lens, we unify a fast-growing and heterogeneous literature, surface stage-specific strengths and gaps, and highlight where current systems fail to compose into robust end-to-end discovery workflows. Because EXHYTE organizes systems by workflow function rather than by agent architecture, the same lens applies to role-partitioned multi-agent scaffolds and to the newer paradigms now entering the field, tool-use systems, standardized tool-access (MCP-style) protocols, coding agents with explicit plan-then-execute loops, and computer-use agents that drive software and instruments through their interfaces. Rather than requiring a new stage for each architecture, these map onto existing substages: tool use corresponds to retrieval and knowledge assembly (E2-E3) and tool-grounded experimental design (T1), plan-then-execute behavior to protocol generation and computational testing (T1–T2), and reflection or critique mechanisms to prioritization and refinement (H2, T2).
Stage-level maturity and bottlenecks
Our synthesis finds that Explore is the most mature stage, driven by rapid progress in literature retrieval, RAG pipelines, knowledge-graph construction, and representation learning. However, this maturity is uneven: most systems treat literature as the primary evidence source, while comparatively few analyze real scientific datasets to identify patterns, anomalies, confounders, or mechanistic gaps that would initiate genuinely data-driven discovery. In contrast, Hypothesize remains underdeveloped beyond generation: many systems can propose ideas, but fewer provide rigorous mechanisms for novelty checking, plausibility assessment, or principled prioritization under explicit constraints. The weakest link remains Hypothesize → Test: translating promising hypotheses into executable experimental plans with reliable evaluation signals and then using those signals to refine or reject hypotheses. The Test stage also lags in practice: most systems remain
in silico
, and the few that incorporate wet-lab validation typically depend on substantial human supervision and bespoke infrastructure. Two further gaps sit at the workflow’s edges rather than within any single stage: trigger formation, problem finding, and assessment of which questions are worth pursuing remain largely human-supplied, since systems enter through human-defined inputs rather than identifying their own problems; and even systems that connect multiple stages stop short of full automation, because evidence interpretation, hypothesis revision, and scientific value judgment still require human checkpoints.
Scope and limitations of EXHYTE as an operational lens
EXHYTE is not intended as a comprehensive theory of all scientific change. It best characterizes data-intensive, tool-mediated inquiry where progress proceeds through iterative exploration, hypothesis formulation, and empirical appraisal. Important dimensions of scientific practice are only partially represented in current systems mapped onto EXHYTE. First, paradigm shifts and other forms of “revolutionary” change involve broader conceptual re-framings and shifts in standards of evidence that are not well captured by present-day computational workflows. Second, scientific knowledge is stabilized through external validation and organized skepticism, including community scrutiny, replication, and credit/prioritization mechanisms, which extend beyond closed-loop internal scoring. Third, human scientific judgment extends well beyond ranking or approving machine-generated outputs: domain intuition, problem selection, interpretive judgment, and contextual understanding shape what counts as a meaningful research question and what constitutes adequate evidence. This last point also carries a risk that grows as workflows automate more substages: heavy reliance on AI for retrieval, idea generation, and appraisal may erode the very capacities—critical reading, independent judgment, and the ability to frame and recognize a worthwhile problem—that these systems presuppose in their human users. We therefore treat the preservation of human judgment not as a temporary scaffold to be removed as systems mature but as a standing requirement for trustworthy discovery. Throughout this survey, we accordingly treat EXHYTE as a pragmatic framework for mapping AI system capabilities and integration points, while explicitly noting where essential social and epistemic mechanisms remain outside the loop.
